Industry News: AI Is Fueling a Newly introduced Startup Boom. Here’s How to Build a Business That Lasts.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a newly introduced entrepreneurial boom.
  • It has been revealed that we’ve seen this before: Fresh technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a newly introduced entrepreneurial boom.

It has been revealed that we’ve seen this before: Fresh technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

It has been revealed that business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for new registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

What’s driving that growth? It’s not a single engine but a combination of forces, including the continued popularity of remote work and the appeal of being your own boss and having more financial freedom, both now more within reach because of AI.

In a recent development, if you previously dropped a business idea because it seemed too complicated or expensive, now may be the time to reconsider. AI has reached a level of capability that didn’t exist just a few years ago. It’s steadily eroding traditional startup barriers, helping founders turn even ambitious ideas into real businesses with less money, fewer employees and fewer outside resources.

Until recently, launching a firm often meant spending money before making money. Office space, equipment, expensive software and employees with specialized skills were requirements in most sectors, not to mention the accountants and consultants needed just to get started.

According to recent reports, now, cloud infrastructure has replaced costly servers. No-code platforms make it possible to build websites and apps without extensive programming knowledge. E-commerce platforms give small companies access to national and global markets. Generative AI accelerates this trend by helping entrepreneurs research markets, analyze competitors, draft business plans, develop marketing campaigns, create content and automate tedious administrative work.

According to recent reports, start by asking yourself, “What do I need to reach customers at this stage, and how will it maximize my return on investment?” Use inexpensive tools to create a product prototype, a landing page or a basic marketing campaign. Talk to potential customers. Test your pricing and measure the response. Save major investments for ideas that show real demand.

Sources indicate that AI gives founders a chance to rethink hiring. Entrepreneurs once had to hire employees or contractors before they were generating enough revenue to support them. Today, a solo founder with the right AI tools can handle many of those functions alone.

In a recent development, that doesn’t mean putting complete trust in a chatbot. AI-assisted work still requires human oversight, judgment, verification and refinement. And when you’re building a trustworthy brand from scratch, you have to consider accuracy, privacy and legal complications.

In a recent development, use AI to draft routine marketing emails, but hire an experienced marketer when strategy matters. Organize basic finances with bookkeeping software, but consult an accountant for important tax decisions. Automate answers to repetitive customer service questions, but keep a human in the loop for complicated interactions or when customers ask for one. The goal isn’t to eliminate employees. It’s to delay fixed expenses until your business can support them.

Industry observers note that historically, founders moved to places like San Francisco or Austin because those cities offered concentrated pools of money and talent. Those hubs remain vibrant, but AI and remote technology are reducing the importance of location.

A tech founder in a small town can use the same AI platforms and cloud services as someone in Silicon Valley. Remote collaboration provides access to talent anywhere, and e-commerce can reach customers far beyond a company’s hometown.

Sources indicate that with AI tools, you can explore many ideas from almost anywhere. Instead of asking, “Where does my business need to be based?” you can ask, “Where would I like to live while I grow my business?” That kind of freedom can make a real difference in your quality of life.

It has been revealed that forming a business and building a successful one are different things. Many of the companies registered this year will never become fully operational. Others will struggle to find customers or stay profitable. AI can’t fix a weak business model, create demand where none exists or eliminate the financial risks of entrepreneurship.

It has been revealed that what AI can do is make the process easier and cheaper, and therein lies the lesson. Instead of investing heavily up front in one untested concept, make a series of small bets. Develop a minimum viable product. Test marketing messages. Experiment with prices. Ask AI to identify the assumptions in your business plan, then test them with real customers and real-world data.

With more than 5 million businesses formed since the start of 2026, the U.S. could finish the year with close to 7 million newly introduced registrations if the current pace continues. There’s evidence that AI may be contributing to that momentum. But like the steam engine, electricity, the internet and smartphones before it, AI is a tool. The real power lies with entrepreneurs who are willing to start lean, test early, automate selectively and spend strategically. With that approach, we may see a boom not only in startups with potential but, more importantly, in businesses that endure.

Privacy coins are poised to be among the biggest cryptocurrency stories of 2027, driven by growing concerns over financial surveillance, institutional adoption, and the future of digital privacy. This creates a compelling investment narrative. Google Gemini AI predicts that two projects, Monero (XMR) and Zcash (ZEC), will stand out, and it aims to forecast which will experience a significant price surge in 2027.

Sources indicate that both Monero and Zcash are established leaders in the privacy-focused cryptocurrency space, but they employ fundamentally different approaches to protecting users’ financial information. Monero offers privacy by default, while Zcash seeks to balance financial confidentiality with greater accessibility for institutional investors.

According to recent reports, as a potential major crypto bull market approaches in 2027, investors may find two distinct opportunities for substantial returns. However, determining which option could deliver the biggest gains may yield surprising results.

Recent findings suggest that monero has long been considered the gold standard for transaction privacy. Unlike conventional cryptocurrencies, where transactions can be publicly inspected on a blockchain, XMR makes privacy an inherent feature of its network.

It achieves this through ring signatures, Ring Confidential Transactions (RingCT), and stealth addresses, which conceal the sender, transaction amount, and recipient. Importantly, privacy is mandatory, not optional.

This gives Monero a compelling proposition as a digital cash alternative, especially as blockchain analytics grow more sophisticated and financial surveillance expands.

Recent findings suggest that however, that same characteristic creates a significant obstacle: regulatory scrutiny. Exchanges in several jurisdictions have restricted or removed XMR trading, potentially limiting access to a broader pool of investors.

Zcash takes a different approach, using zero-knowledge cryptography to enable shielded transactions while retaining the option of transparent transactions.

Its shielded addresses let users conceal transaction details, while viewing keys let them selectively disclose information to auditors or other authorized parties. This flexibility could prove particularly attractive to institutions that want privacy without completely sacrificing compliance.

The distinction could become increasingly key as institutional investors look beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum for opportunities in specialized crypto sectors.

Privacy coins are already attracting attention beyond their traditional communities. Zcash has made considerable progress in positioning itself as a more institutionally accessible privacy network, with regulated investment products emerging and interest in its underlying technology growing.

Meanwhile, Monero continues to benefit from its established reputation, consistent privacy guarantees and decentralized architecture.

Industry observers note that the broader investment narrative is also changing. As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more transactions become visible to blockchain analytics companies, incentivizing individuals and businesses to seek greater financial confidentiality.

However, the regulatory landscape could become a major obstacle in 2027. The EU’s Anti-Money Laundering Regulation is scheduled to apply from July 10, 2027, with restrictions covering crypto-asset accounts involving anonymity-enhancing coins.

Recent findings suggest that crucially, the legislation’s definition encompasses privacy features that operate either systematically or optionally. This means neither project can assume its architecture provides an exemption.

Looking beyond daily price fluctuations, the weekly and monthly charts will be particularly crucial in determining which cryptocurrency has the strongest potential heading into 2027.

Recent findings suggest that for Monero, the key technical consideration is whether it can establish a sustained higher-high structure following its previous major market cycle. A successful retest of former resistance zones as support could lay the groundwork for another substantial move, particularly if capital rotates toward privacy-focused assets.

XMR also benefits from a relatively predictable supply model. Its permanent tail emission produces 0.6 XMR every two minutes, with an inflation rate that gradually declines over time.

In a recent development, zcash, meanwhile, has a more conventional fixed supply of 21 million coins, giving it a familiar scarcity narrative. Its longer-term technical outlook will depend heavily on whether it can maintain gains tied to its growing institutional profile and establish stronger historical support.

Both could benefit enormously from a broader cryptocurrency bull market, although ZEC’s previous outperformance means investors should also consider the possibility of profit-taking and deeper corrections.

Sources indicate that there are compelling arguments for both projects, but their potential price trajectories could look quite different. In an optimistic 2027 scenario, Zcash could target a broad trading range of $1,600–$2,400, supported by institutional demand, increased shielded transaction adoption, and a stronger position within the privacy sector.

Monero could potentially push towards $900–$1,400, with a particularly bullish scenario opening the door to even higher valuations if demand for censorship-resistant digital cash accelerates.

It has been revealed that these are speculative price scenarios, not technical guarantees, and regulatory restrictions remain a substantial risk for both projects. Nevertheless, one vital consideration could give XMR the advantage: its established position as a dedicated privacy currency.

Zcash arguably has the stronger institutional narrative, but Monero arguably has the stronger proposition for users who consider financial privacy non-negotiable. If that distinction becomes increasingly key during the next market cycle, demand for XMR could accelerate considerably.

While Zcash could continue attracting institutional capital and potentially deliver impressive returns, I believe Monero has the ingredients for a stronger percentage gain over the longer term.

Its established reputation, mandatory privacy architecture, and potential to benefit from renewed demand for financial anonymity make it an intriguing candidate. If privacy becomes one of crypto’s defining investment narratives in 2027, XMR could be one of the biggest beneficiaries.

Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • According to recent reports, for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

According to recent reports, for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Industry observers note that most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

It has been revealed that those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

It has been revealed that denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

In a recent development, timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

According to recent reports, this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

It has been revealed that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Recent findings suggest that node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

In a recent development, this is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams strategy to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec indicates it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

It has been revealed that the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Sources indicate that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

  • This decision comes after over a year of regulatory filings and multiple delays.
  • It has been revealed that as per the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Investment firm Roundhill has suddenly terminated plans to launch two newly introduced XRP- and Solana (SOL)-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

This decision comes after over a year of regulatory filings and multiple delays.

It has been revealed that as per the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings on Nov. 18, Roundhill has officially withdrawn plans to launch the Roundhill XRP Covered Call Strategy ETF and Roundhill Solana Covered Call Strategy ETF.

Interestingly, it submitted the applications for these two funds on Oct. 17, 2025. Therefore, these two funds had been awaiting launch for over 13 months.

As per the latest regulatory filings, Roundhill has been consistently delaying the effective dates for these two funds.

However, instead of launching them, the investment firm has decided to drop both products.

In its requests to withdraw the filings for these funds, Roundhill revealed that it "has no further intention to pursue effectiveness of the Fund." The firm noted that it had not sold any shares under the registrations for these two funds.

Intriguingly, Roundhill failed to elaborate on the sudden decision to axe its plans to launch these two ETFs.

Roundhill was planning to launch income-generating XRP and Solana ETFs using a covered call strategy. In such a strategy, investors sell options to earn premiums while also maintaining exposure to the price movements of XRP and Solana.

Unlike spot-based ETFs, these funds would not have held the cryptocurrencies directly. Instead, they would have used options written against existing cryptocurrency ETFs.

According to recent reports, A covered call strategy can be useful for generating regular income. However, it can also cap profits during strong market rallies.

Notably, there has been relatively low demand for income-generating cryptocurrency investment products. This raises concerns about investors' interest in these ETFs.

Surprisingly, this decision came amid substantial net inflows into spot-based XRP and Solana ETFs.

U.S. spot XRP and Solana ETFs recorded net inflows of roughly $969 million between May and October 2026, according to data from SoSoValue.

Overall, these spot ETFs held around $3.26 billion in assets under management as of the end of October.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Sources indicate that orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

In a recent development, the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, mentioned in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

Sources indicate that “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

According to recent reports, the startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

It has been revealed that orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

Industry observers note that the Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the manufacturer said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

According to recent reports, the startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that most entrepreneurs are using AI to get work done faster. But what if it’s moving their businesses in the wrong direction?

In a recent development, AI can now help entrepreneurs produce marketing campaigns, research competitors, develop strategies and complete work that once took entire teams. It’s an extraordinary shift in what’s possible for a small business. But there’s a hidden risk in all that productivity. In the video above, I explore why the entrepreneurs who gain the greatest advantage from AI aren’t the ones doing more work, but the ones discovering opportunities everyone else overlooks.

In a recent development, that’s what I call the “Progress Illusion.” When AI makes completing tasks effortless, it’s tempting to mistake activity for achievement. But there’s a difference between the work AI completes, how customers respond, the business results that follow and the longer-term consequences. These are the four dominoes that determine whether all that activity is actually moving your business forward.

Finished is a status. Progress is a consequence.

Sources indicate that consider a surprising study of eBay’s paid search advertising. When the tech giant stopped running ads for searches containing its own name, researchers found that 99.5% of the lost paid-ad traffic was replaced by free search traffic. Now imagine using AI to scale that campaign because the dashboard looked impressive. You wouldn’t necessarily be scaling growth. You could be scaling waste.

The opportunity for entrepreneurs is to use AI for something far more powerful than execution: strategic foresight.

According to recent reports, in the video, I walk through AHEAD, my five-step framework for challenging assumptions, exploring upcoming possibilities and uncovering business opportunities you might otherwise overlook. But even smart analysis has its limits. AI can generate so many competing strategies that deciding what to do becomes a job in itself. That’s the “Analysis Trap.”.

Recent findings suggest that the solution is knowing when to stop researching and start acting. I call it the “Decision Line”: three questions that help you determine whether you need stronger evidence or whether it’s time to make your next move.

Sources indicate that because your most valuable opportunity might not be the one you’re already pursuing. It could be an entirely different direction you haven’t considered. And you don’t need a Fortune 500 strategy department to start thinking more strategically about your business.

Recent findings suggest that AI can help you execute almost any plan. The real competitive advantage is discovering which plan deserves to be executed.

And in the video above, I’ll show you how to start thinking differently, uncover opportunities others overlook and make your next business move with greater confidence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The organization states revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero.
  • The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.
  • Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The organization states revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero.

The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.

Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.

Sources indicate that I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns.

OpenAI’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million owners and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users.

Sources indicate that by contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, introduced just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1, the firm says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record.

In a recent development, anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the organization can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it states it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology.

Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets:.

Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn-led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the manufacturer at $965 billion.

Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google, Amazon, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow.

Recent findings suggest that the AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of latest wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension.

The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It notes its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services.

That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses.

Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption.

Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company indicates it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance.

As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.

In a recent development, RLUSD is issued by Standard Custody & Trust under the supervision of the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), and its reserves are held at custodian bank BNY. In the fall, RLUSD received a Moody's rating and was listed on Coinbase and Robinhood, and Ripple received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to launch Ripple National Trust Bank.

Ripple has also integrated RLUSD with payment providers Arf, Convera and Cross River Bank, and the stablecoin is now used in dollar settlements between companies.

In a CNBC interview on Nov. 19, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse called blockchain-based transactions "a wave of emerging technology." "I think 10 years from now you'll see blockchain implemented across our financial infrastructure," he said.

Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

Sources indicate that that’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a fresh company with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

In a recent development, the startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

It has been revealed that youTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

Industry observers note that “When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, mentioned. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

In a recent development, some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise notes its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

It has been revealed that clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

Sources indicate that “Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan remarked. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

It has been revealed that so far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

“It was really notable that he had full control,” Morgan noted. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

#76153. This Is the Reason Your AI Tools Actually Remember Anything

This Is the Reason Your AI Tools Actually Remember Anything

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • During the World Cup this year, I built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot.
  • Two quick definitions before we go further, since neither tool is exactly a household name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

During the World Cup this year, I built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot. From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. What I learned building it applies to almost any AI product that has to stay fast, cheap and accurate at the same time.

Two quick definitions before we go further, since neither tool is exactly a household name. Redis is “an open-source, in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, message broker and streaming engine,” most commonly used in AI products as a fast cache that stores one exact answer under one exact label. RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation, is defined by AWS as “a technique used to augment a large language model (LLM) with external data, such as a tech giant’s internal documents.” Instead of matching an exact label, it searches for a broader knowledge base using meaning rather than exact wording. Redis is precise and cheap but rigid. RAG is more flexible and durable, but costs more to run.

My first move wasn’t a vector database, it was a Redis cache built around a simple labeling rule: Identical requests get an identical key, something like the football matchup Argentina vs. Spain. The savings were immediate. As I documented in my LinkedIn article on Rune Score, “without the cache, a fresh extraction followed by an analysis can consume up to 23,000 input tokens: scraped content, context, history. With a cache that hits the same key, that number drops to about 5,000 tokens,” a 4.5-fold reduction in the single most expensive part of the pipeline.

According to recent reports, AI cost usually comes from what you repeat unnecessarily. If 10 people ask your product the same question within a reasonable time window, rerunning the full, expensive pipeline 10 times is money burned for no reason.

People don’t talk in fixed labels. They might write “FC Barcelona vs Real Madrid,” or “Barça – Madrid,” and a strict cache treats each variant as a completely different request. That means duplicate work, a missed answer that was already sitting there or an unnecessary rerun of the whole expensive pipeline just because the wording didn’t match.

It has been revealed that this is where RAG earns its place, through a technique called embeddings. According to Google Cloud’s documentation, “the closer objects are in the embedding space, the more semantically similar they are, and greater distances indicate greater semantic dissimilarity.” In plain terms, a knowledge base built this way can retrieve a past answer even when the question is worded completely differently, because it searches by meaning rather than exact wording.

Industry observers note that here’s a lesson worth internalizing regardless of what you’re building: The biggest quality bottleneck in a RAG system usually isn’t the retrieval technology itself; it’s what feeds it. This is the classic computing idea that TechTarget defines as garbage in, garbage out, or GIGO, “the idea that in any system, the quality of output is determined by the quality of the input.” In my pipeline, every time I cut corners on how much content got extracted from a source, the resulting analysis got visibly worse downstream.

Sources indicate that the same logic applies to how the system ranks relevance. Trusting a single relevance score is fragile. Redis’s own engineering blog puts it plainly: “the consistent takeaway across these studies is that combining retrievers tends to surface more relevant results in the top positions than either method on its own.” Combining exact keyword matches, meaning-based search and how recent the information is, then merging those into one ranking, beats relying on any single signal alone.

In my experiment with Rune Score, RAG hit brings a request down from 20,000 to 8,000 tokens — a 60% reduction. Compared to the 80% reduction from an exact Redis hit, that’s less economical and slightly slower, but that gap isn’t a strike against RAG. What it buys instead is tolerance for how people actually phrase things, memory that outlives a cache’s expiration window and an architecture that’s reusable well beyond the one product you built it for.

Redis and RAG aren’t competing choices; they’re sequential ones. The best refactor isn’t the one that’s theoretically right; it’s the one that lets you roll back in seconds if the real metrics don’t hold up. Build the cheap, fast cache first, let it teach you what your users actually ask for and only then invest in a full retrieval system for the cases a cache structurally can’t handle.

Latest Update: StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a fresh round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

According to recent reports, stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The firm has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

According to recent reports, the problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

Industry observers note that it gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has remarked the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

In a recent development, it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor mentioned up to 5,000 consumers may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

According to recent reports, how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

In a recent development, more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

In a recent development, growth spurt: StepSecurity indicates its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The tech giant has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity looks to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company notes it also looks to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

Industry observers note that the offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the firm.

Industry observers note that anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a firm making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the manufacturer had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

It has been revealed that anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

In a recent development, as of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed prepares for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the firm and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. Forty-six attorneys general have joined a Latest York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials unveiled this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the firm’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” indicates one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

It has been revealed that the result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she claims. One venture manager who reappeared too promptly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

In a recent development, softBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it debuted a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

#76149. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1904 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Sources indicate that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Sources indicate that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

Recent findings suggest that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the organization has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella stated, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Recent findings suggest that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

Industry observers note that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a manufacturer partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in substantial, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

It has been revealed that since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

Industry observers note that what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the firm with reports.

In a recent development, the first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from latest finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

It has been revealed that moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

It has been revealed that no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

According to recent reports, since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

It has been revealed that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple owners to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security problem involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Sources indicate that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Recent findings suggest that here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Recent findings suggest that managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

It has been revealed that even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

According to recent reports, it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

Recent findings suggest that it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solana has remained one of the major cryptocurrencies that have been heavily affected by the persistent crypto market volatility, stalling demand from both retail and institutional investors.

While Solana has continued to struggle amid the growing market uncertainty, it appears that traders are increasingly exiting their positions even across its DeFi market.

Recent data showcased by blockchain monitoring platform Lookonchain shows that two Solana whales unstaked a total of 2.31 million SOL on November 19.

While the total amount of SOL unstaked was worth about $169.4 million, further data showed that the whales proceeded to transfer the tokens to Coinbase, a leading cryptocurrency exchange in the U.S.

It is notable to note that the act of withdrawing SOL previously committed to the network's staking mechanism is regarded as unstaking.

While this move automatically gives holders the ability to transfer, sell, or use the unstaked tokens, the massive unstaking of 2.31 million SOL from large holders has drawn attention within the crypto community regarding the intention behind the move.

With curiosity on the rise about the whales' decision to move such a large amount of SOL to Coinbase Prime, the timing of the move has triggered speculation that the whales may be intending to sell the tokens.

Notably, the move arrived when Solana was trading around $74, briefly shifting into green territory just a few days after it retested $67, the lowest level seen since June 2026.

Since the prolonged price correction has continued to weaken investor confidence, it appears that the whales have acted upon the growing fear and withdrawn the assets they had initially committed to the Solana network to hedge against further losses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that that WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a new Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before. As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”.

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a newly introduced factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

Sources indicate that the CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

Recent findings suggest that it happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).
